profile.headline: Software Engineer at Teradyne
profile.summary:
Experienced Software Engineer with over 5 years' experience including working in the semiconductor industry with background in computational chemistry, mathematical modeling, data analysis, and scientific research. 
Skilled in C++, object-oriented programming, Python, shell scripting, and debugging. MS focused in Computer Science and Engineering from Santa Clara University.

positions.title: Senior Software Engineer
positions.description:
-Designed and implemented device drivers in C++ for semiconductor automated test equipment (ATE)
- Proactively conducted comprehensive code reviews of features, bug fixes, and documentation to prevent software defects. 
- Wrote thorough unit tests in C++ to ensure code coverage and rapidly catch and resolve regressions.
- Proficiently utilized code profiler for test time analysis, debugging, and identification of code segments necessitating refactoring.
- Collaborated with cross-functional teams to diagnose and resolve CURI software issues, facilitating communication between semiconductor automated test equipment (ATE) and probers/handlers via GPIB, Serial, or TTL.  This involved debugging multi-threaded processes.

projects.title: Analyzing thermostability of the engrailed homeodomain and an engineered variant using molecular dynamics simulations
projects.description: Computational biology research project with Dr. Michelle McCully funded by the DeNardo Science Scholars award at Santa Clara University.  Molecular dynamics (MD) is a theoretical physics technique which allows us to study molecular systems with detail at the atomic level.  All atom molecular dynamics simulations treat every atom explicitly including solvating water molecules during calculations, which is the most realistic.  Achieving this level of detail is computationally expensive, so we study small ultrafast folding proteins with molecular dynamics.  We performed the MD simulations using the NAMD software and performed analysis using the ilmm software and Python and Bash scripts.  Presented results at the Biophysical Society conference in 2018, and published in Biophysical Journal https://www.cell.com/biophysj/fulltext/S0006-3495(19)30028-1

projects.title: Finding classes of identifiable linear compartment models using graph theory
projects.description: Mathematics research project with Professor Nicolette Meshkat funded by the Clare Boothe Luce Undergraduate Research award.  My summer research was in an area of mathematical biology called parameter identifiability, which concerns which unknown parameters of a model can be determined from given input-output data.  If all of the parameters can be determined from perfect input-output data, we say the model is identifiable.  However, if the parameters can take on an infinite number of values and yet yield the same input-output data, we say the model is unidentifiable.  Linear compartment models are used in pharmacokinetics, toxicology, cell biology, physiology, and ecology.  I wrote a program in Mathematica to implement algorithms for testing identifiability of a particular model.  I presented a poster at the MAA Golden Section Meeting in 2017 and gave a talk at the Northern California Undergraduate Mathematics Conference.
